Three ideas carry most of the R in this course. R stores things in **objects**,
you do things with **functions**, and the commonest object is a **vector**. Run
the cells, change the numbers, and try things that might not work.

## Objects

`<-` is the assignment arrow. It puts the thing on its right into the name on
its left.

```{webr}
n_screened <- 2400
district   <- "Kolar"

n_screened
district
```

Nothing printed when you assigned. R stored the value silently. Typing the name
on its own line is what prints it.

Change `2400` to a number from your own work and run it again.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
You will see `=` used for assignment in other people's code. It mostly works.
Use `<-` anyway: it is the convention, and `=` means something different inside
a function call, which is exactly where beginners get caught.
:::

## Functions

A function is a verb. It takes **arguments** in brackets, separated by commas,
and gives back a value.

```{webr}
sqrt(144)
round(3.14159, 2)
nchar("epidemiology")
```

`round(3.14159, 2)` passed 2 arguments: the number, and how many decimal
places. Most confusion about R functions is confusion about which argument is
which.

You can name arguments, and then the order stops mattering:

```{webr}
round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2)
round(digits = 2, x = 3.14159)
```

## Vectors

A vector is several values of the same type in a row. `c()` combines them. The
`c` is for *combine*.

```{webr}
# Malaria cases notified in six consecutive months
cases <- c(14, 22, 31, 27, 19, 11)

cases
length(cases)
```

Functions applied to a vector work on every element at once. There is no loop to
write.

```{webr}
cases <- c(14, 22, 31, 27, 19, 11)

sum(cases)
mean(cases)
max(cases)
range(cases)
```

Arithmetic works the same way. This is **vectorisation**, and it is why R code
for data work is usually short.

```{webr}
cases      <- c(14, 22, 31, 27, 19, 11)
population <- c(12000, 12000, 12500, 12500, 13000, 13000)

# cases per 1000 population, month by month
cases / population * 1000
```

Six divisions, one line, no loop.

## Types

A vector holds one type. The 3 you will meet most often:

```{webr}
counts   <- c(14, 22, 31)                       # numeric
district <- c("Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan")      # character
exposed  <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)                # logical

class(counts)
class(district)
class(exposed)
```

Mix them and R quietly converts everything to the most forgiving type, usually
character. This is a common source of "why is my column text?".

```{webr}
mixed <- c(14, "Kolar", TRUE)
mixed
class(mixed)
```

Look at what happened: `14` became `"14"`, with quotation marks. You can no
longer take its mean.

## Comparison, and why logicals matter

Comparing a vector gives you a logical vector, one answer per element.

```{webr}
# Ages of 8 participants
age <- c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45, 19, 58, 40)

age >= 45
```

And a logical vector sums as if `TRUE` were 1 and `FALSE` were 0. So `sum()`
counts, and `mean()` gives a proportion.

```{webr}
age <- c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45, 19, 58, 40)

sum(age >= 45)     # how many
mean(age >= 45)    # what proportion
```

That second line is prevalence in miniature. Hold on to it.

## Missing values

Real data has holes. R writes a hole as `NA`, and it is contagious on purpose:
the mean of a set of numbers you do not fully know is not knowable.

```{webr}
sbp <- c(128, 142, NA, 136, 151, NA, 119)

mean(sbp)
```

You get `NA`, not an error. R is telling you the answer depends on the 2 values
you do not have.

To average only the ones you do have, say so:

```{webr}
sbp <- c(128, 142, NA, 136, 151, NA, 119)

mean(sbp, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(is.na(sbp))     # how many are missing
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `na.rm = TRUE` is a decision, not a fix
It changes the question. You asked for the mean of 7 people. You now have the
mean of the 5 you measured.

Sometimes that is fine. Sometimes the 2 missing people are missing *because*
they were the sickest. Then it is not fine. Ask why the values are missing
before you drop them.
:::

## Exercises

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: your first vector"}
**Time:** 4 minutes

A screening camp measured fasting blood glucose in five people: 96, 110, 142,
88 and 125 mg/dL. Put those into a vector called `glucose`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_vector
glucose <- ______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_vector
#| solution: true
glucose <- c(96, 110, 142, 88, 125)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_vector
#| check: true
if (identical(as.numeric(.result), c(96, 110, 142, 88, 125))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — a numeric vector of five readings.")
} else if (is.character(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Those are text, not numbers. Drop the quotation marks.")
} else if (length(.result) != 5) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You need all five readings, in the order given.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use c() to combine the five values: c(96, 110, ...).")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_vector"}
`c()` combines values. They go inside the brackets, separated by commas, with
no quotation marks because they are numbers.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: count the raised readings"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Using the same five readings, count how many are **126 mg/dL or above** — the
usual fasting threshold for diabetes. Note that 126 itself would count.

Compare the whole vector at once, then sum the result.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_count
glucose <- c(96, 110, 142, 88, 125)

______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_count
#| solution: true
glucose <- c(96, 110, 142, 88, 125)

sum(glucose >= 126)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_count
#| check: true
if (identical(as.numeric(.result), 1)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — one reading, 142, is 126 or above.")
} else if (is.logical(.result) && length(.result) == 5) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the comparison itself: five TRUE/FALSE answers. Wrap it in sum() to count them.")
} else if (identical(as.numeric(.result), 0.2)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the proportion. mean() gives a proportion; sum() gives a count. Here we want the count.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Compare the whole vector at once with glucose >= 126, then pass that to sum().")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_count"}
`glucose >= 126` gives you five `TRUE`/`FALSE` answers. `sum()` of those counts
the `TRUE`s, because `TRUE` counts as 1.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 3: a mean with a hole in it"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Haemoglobin was measured in six women, but two results were lost:
11.2, NA, 9.8, 12.6, NA, 10.4 g/dL.

Find the mean of the four values you do have, rounded to one decimal place.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_namean
hb <- c(11.2, NA, 9.8, 12.6, NA, 10.4)

______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_namean
#| solution: true
hb <- c(11.2, NA, 9.8, 12.6, NA, 10.4)

round(mean(hb, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_namean
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 11))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — 11.0 g/dL across the four women measured. Note what that number is NOT: the mean for all six.")
} else if (length(.result) == 1 && is.na(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You got NA. R will not average numbers it does not know. Add na.rm = TRUE inside mean().")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 7.333333, tolerance = 1e-4))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You divided by six. mean(hb, na.rm = TRUE) divides by the four values that exist, not by all six slots.")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right shape, wrong number. Take mean(hb, na.rm = TRUE) and then round it to 1 decimal place.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You want a single number: mean() with na.rm = TRUE, wrapped in round(..., 1).")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_namean"}
Two steps. `mean(hb, na.rm = TRUE)` gets the average of what is there. Then
`round(that, 1)` trims it to one decimal place.
:::
:::

## What you should now be able to do

- Store a value in a name with `<-`, and print it by typing the name.
- Call a function with positional or named arguments.
- Build a vector with `c()`, and apply a function to all of it at once.
- Recognise the three common types, and why mixing them turns numbers to text.
- Count and take proportions with `sum()` and `mean()` over a comparison.
- See `NA` for what it is, and decide about it deliberately.
